title: NP-hardness of three-manifold homeomorphism
formal: Is homeomorphism of connected compact triangulated 3-manifolds NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Use the domain \(\mathcal D\) below, allowing boundary and nonorientable manifolds. Equivalently, is there one uniform polynomial-time Turing machine \(R\) which, on every binary string \(x\), outputs a valid pair \((T_x,U_x)\in\mathcal D\), such that \[x\in\mathrm{3SAT}\iff H(T_x,U_x)?\] Outputs must satisfy the manifold promise on both satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs.
why: NP-hardness would locate a central topological classification task relative to general combinatorial search. It would supply a stronger complexity obstruction than the currently known reduction from graph isomorphism.
status_note: The NP-hardness question is open in the checked 2024 report, and the 2025 discussion retains graph-isomorphism hardness as the known comparison. The bounded search through 14 September 2026 found no valid-output NP-hardness resolution for the stated target.

importance.reason: A major lower-bound question for topological equivalence, asking whether general NP computation can be encoded in valid pairs of 3-manifolds.

sentences: Deciding whether two triangulated three-manifolds are homeomorphic has algorithms, but decidability alone says little about feasible running time.
This question seeks an NP-hardness lower bound for the general decision problem.
A reduction would have to encode arbitrary instances of a known hard problem into pairs of manifolds.
Hardness of related knot or triangulation optimization tasks does not immediately supply that encoding.
Such a result would locate manifold equivalence more precisely among familiar computational problems and constrain expectations for general-purpose recognition algorithms.

definitions: A triangulation consists of \(t\geq1\) labelled copies of \(\Delta^3=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=0}^3x_i=1\}\), with some triangular faces paired by affine bijections specified by permutations of their three vertices. Each face is unpaired or paired with one other face; a pairing to the identical face slot is forbidden, pairings are reciprocal, and different faces of the same tetrahedron may be paired. The realization \(|T|\) is the disjoint union of the tetrahedra modulo the stated identifications, with the quotient topology. The input promise is that each realization is a nonempty connected compact 3-manifold, possibly with boundary: every point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of \(\mathbb R^3\) or of \(\mathbb R^2\times[0,\infty)\). Orientability is not promised and no orientation, boundary marking or distinguished submanifold is supplied. Homeomorphism means a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, with no orientation-preserving or boundary-label requirement. In dimension three this agrees with equivalence of PL triangulations; combinatorial isomorphism of the supplied tetrahedron lists is not required. For a concrete binary encoding, write \(t\) in unary followed by the \(4t\) face slots in label order, each recording an unpaired flag or a partner tetrahedron index, a two-bit face index and one of the six vertex permutations; tetrahedron indices use \(\lceil\log_2(t+1)\rceil\) bits. The two encodings are concatenated and their total bit length is \(N\). Let \(\mathcal D\) be the promised domain of such pairs and \(H(T,U)\) the assertion \(|T|\cong|U|\). Algorithms and verifiers are uniform deterministic multitape Turing machines with bit-operation cost, no advice, oracles or randomness. The certificate statements concern this promised domain: verifiers must halt in their polynomial time bound on all bit strings, but acceptance outside \(\mathcal D\) has no specified topological meaning. The language \(\mathrm{3SAT}\) consists of encodings of satisfiable conjunctions of clauses containing at most three literals, where a literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. Variable indices and the entire clause list are explicitly encoded in binary; malformed strings are outside the language. A many-one reduction returns one pair, with its entire length and construction time bounded by a polynomial in \(|x|\). It does not query a homeomorphism oracle or obtain a sequence of adaptive answers. The verifier machinery in the common domain description is not an extra NP-membership assumption on homeomorphism. Since 3SAT is NP-complete, the stated valid-output reduction gives a reduction from every NP language to this promised problem.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that such a valid-output reduction exists, or that no such deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction exists. A positive result must establish the polynomial resource bound, validity of every output manifold and both directions of the satisfiability/homeomorphism equivalence. A negative result must exclude all reductions of this kind. NP-hardness of a related knot, embedding or triangulation-optimization task is insufficient without a reduction to this exact equivalence question. No proof that homeomorphism belongs to NP is required for the positive answer.

context_blocks.text: Schleimer’s Question 5, attributed there to Burton, asks for NP-hardness of Homeo(3). This card fixes polynomial-time many-one reductions and requires valid triangulated manifolds on every output.

NP-hardness is a lower-bound comparison: any polynomial-time algorithm for homeomorphism would then decide every NP language in polynomial time. It does not assert NP membership, and hence does not by itself assert NP-completeness.
Lackenby establishes hardness relative to graph isomorphism through a many-one reduction to closed 3-manifold homeomorphism. Graph-isomorphism hardness alone is not the required NP-hardness theorem.

Kuperberg’s elementary-recursive algorithm concerns closed oriented manifolds and provides an upper bound on decision complexity. Such an upper bound is compatible with NP-hardness; decidability and NP-hardness are not mutually exclusive.

The yes/no orientation of the reduction matters. A transformation that sends satisfiable formulas to nonhomeomorphic pairs would instead compare SAT with the complement problem. Likewise, allowing invalid geometric outputs would evade the promised decision task.

A positive answer together with a general NP certificate theorem would make the promised homeomorphism problem NP-complete under valid-output reductions. Combined instead with a coNP certificate theorem, it would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). These consequences explain why the three questions are retained separately.
